source: Open pipes resonate at fₙ = nv/(2L); pipes closed at one end only at odd multiples of v/(4L).
Students give a pipe closed at one end the same set of harmonics as an open pipe.

Flutes, organ pipes and clarinets make music with standing sound waves in air columns. The idea is the same as for strings, but the ends work differently. As in Sound: Pitch and Loudness, sound is air moving back and forth along the pipe.

Open at both ends (all harmonics): $$f_n = \frac{nv}{2L}, \quad n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$$ Closed at one end (odd harmonics only): $$f_n = \frac{nv}{4L}, \quad n = 1, 3, 5, \dots$$ A closed end is a displacement node; an open end is a displacement antinode.
A pipe closed at one end in its third harmonic: a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.

Air can't move through a closed end, so it is a node. At an open end the air moves freely, so it is an antinode. Open–open: antinode to antinode, a whole number of half wavelengths, just like a string. Closed–open: node to antinode, an odd number of quarter wavelengths, $L = n\frac{\lambda}{4}$ with $n$ odd. The even ones would need a node at the open end, which can't happen.

Giving a pipe closed at one end the same harmonics as an open pipe. A closed pipe has only odd multiples of its fundamental, and its fundamental is half that of an open pipe of the same length. Check: closed-pipe frequencies like $150, 250, 350\ \text{Hz}$ step by $2f_1$, and $f_1 = 50\ \text{Hz}$ itself is half the step.
Find the first two resonant frequencies of a $0.50\ \text{m}$ pipe ($v = 343\ \text{m/s}$), first open at both ends, then closed at one end.
A pipe resonates at $150$, $250$ and $350\ \text{Hz}$, and at no frequencies between them. Is it open or closed at one end? How long is it? ($v = 343\ \text{m/s}$.)
Closed at one end, about $1.7\ \text{m}$ long
Neighbors differ by $100\ \text{Hz}$. If it were open, the frequencies would be multiples of $100$, but $150$ is not.
They are $3, 5, 7$ times $50\ \text{Hz}$: odd multiples, so the pipe is closed at one end with $f_1 = 50\ \text{Hz}$.
